column5: I would suggest including docstrings for all functions (for internal functions, the docstrings don't need to be extensive, but should give some idea of the purpose of the function). Also, I think it is cleaner to import all needed packages at the beginning of the code file, rather than scattered throughout.
column6: I found the report to be very readable with no notable grammar issues.
column7: There is a narrative throughout as to whether the groups are separate or on a continuum. Overall, the sections feel connected to me.
column8: The data cleaning section is very nicely done, with cleaning steps described clearly with an appropriate amount of detail, and all choices are justified. I particularly like the observation that there are only missing answers for earlier IDs, suggesting that the survey may have later required an answer (nice sleuthing!).
column9: I liked that they used 1x1 degree aggregated data, which is more digestable than mapping individual respondents but still preserves fine-scale spatial variation. I don't think that a chi-squared test was necessary for this exploratory section.
column10: I liked that they used an "all other answers" category for the maps, it helped keep them clean and digestable.
column11: For fig. 3 it would have been nice to have the colors match between the maps. For example, blue go with grandma and grandpa, red go with other for both, etc. It would have been easier to connect the two maps that way. Additionally, I did not find fig. 2 to be informative; I think it would have left out of the final report.
column12: I liked that they tried PCA using both with and without SD-scaling (they explained well why you may or may not want to do scaling here). And that they also considered t-SNE. I think it could have been useful to look at the dimension reductions colored by region (West, South, Midwest, Northeast), rather than (or in addition to) by latitude/longitude.
column13: Overall, I think the figures are nicely and clearly labeled throughout this section, which is important when there are different methods and standardization choices happening.
column14: For the cumulative % of variation plot (fig. 5), I think it would have been nice to show the curve across all components rather than just the first 20. That would have allowed you to explore, for example, how many components are needed to explain 80% of the variation. Also, for side-by-side plots, reducing repetition would be cleaner (e.g., you don't need two legends for cumulative and the y-axis labeled separately for both).
column15: For the choice of methods, K-means was definitely appropriate. I don't know enough about GMM to comment on the appropriateness in this context. They used the first 20 PCs, but this decision wasn't justified based on the amount of variation explained. In fact, only about 30% of the variation is explained by the first 20 PCs, which is not very much. You would likely want to select the number of PCs based on a target % of variation explained (maybe 75/80). For both methods they did reasonably justify their choice for the number of clusters (although it is not clear if the silhouette score is for K-means or GMM).
column16: For fig. 10, I liked the idea of having the squares lighter where the cluster is less dominant. I think it's useful to retain the information in the map. (Although the gradient could be made to be more distinct, it was a bit hard to tell which squares were supposed to be lighter).
column17: For fig. 10, it would have been nice to use cluster names in the map (such as Northeast). This would have made a nice connection between the map and table 3.
column18: I think the stability analysis is reasonable, looking at both different starting points and bootstrapping. They used adjusted Rand Index to compare cluster results, which is appropriate. I don't think fig. 12 is particularly useful and could have been excluded from the final report (the text explaining the values in the figure is more informative).
